messages.author: ea61eb17436b9dde
messages.subject: Basic question: "cor.ov"
parts:
Hi everybody,

maybe this shouldn't even be a question and I'm just missing the obvious, but here it goes:

For my sem model I also administered the command inspect(fit, what = "cor.ov"), which, as I understood it, should give me the correlation between my model variables.
Since I have several models with a bunch of mediators I also wanted to include a correlation matrix that shows the correlation between all the constructs across models. In order to do so I used the R Commander and had it create the Pearson's correlation and corresponding p-values.

Now my question: The output from the inspect() command doesn't match my correlations obtained from the regular correlation matrix. Could somebody tell me why and which ones I should rather use?
(While we're at it, R Commander also produced the adjusted p-values with Holm's method, after searching the internet, I am half-convinced that I should just use the regular ones, but if anyone has feelings about that as well, I am happy to hear them)

Thank You, You help is hugely appreciated!

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Basic question: "cor.ov"
parts:
"cor.ov" provides the model-implied correlations among observed variables in the model.  "cor.lv" provides the model-implied correlations among the latent constructs in the model.  "cor.all" provides the model-implied correlations among observed and latent variables in the model, so you can get the so-called "Structure Matrix".  All of these are calculated using model parameters, not the observed correlations.  "sampstat" provides the observed covariance matrix and mean vector, to which the model was fit. If you extract that and use the cov2cor() function to convert the covariance matrix to a correlation matrix, you should see matching results (unless you have missing data).

I'm not sure why you are concerned with significance tests of the correlations, but those are a function of sample size as well as effect size.  SEM is a way for you to impose a structure that explains why variables are correlated, so although it is recommended to provide the sufficient statistics (means, correlations, and SDs) so that others can reproduce your model results, it is not necessary to test each correlation against a null hypothesis that it is zero in the population.  But if you do, then adjusting the p values for multiple testing is just a way for you to keep the familywise Type I error rate low.  You could read about other methods in the ?p.adjust help page.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Basic question: "cor.ov"
parts: Just to be sure, so "model-implied" means this is how they should correlate if my model was correct?
Yes, if the parameter estimates are the true population values, then the model-implied correlations are the population correlations.

So if I don't have explicit hypotheses regarding the correlations I shouldn't report whether or not they were significant? I figured since a relationship between the variables is to some extent the basis of my regressional assumptions, it would make sense to do so.

I don't think any reviewer would expect you to do both a correlation and regression analysis on the same variables.  A simple regression slope will have the same p value as bivariate correlation because a correlation is a standardized regression slope.  But once you have multiple predictors of an outcome, then you have potential multicollinearity and suppression that make regression slopes more analogous to semipartial correlations.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Basic question: "cor.ov"
parts: Is it safe to assume that the inclusion of predictors (all time-invariant) is the reason for the discrepancy?

Yes, the parameter estimates are covariances between residuals, so standardized estimates are partial correlations, not the zero-order (model-implied) correlations you get from lavInspect(fit. "cor.lv").  In an unconditional model, they are the same because the residual variance == the total variance.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Basic question: "cor.ov"
parts: when you have missing data, does the correlation provided by lavInspect() use FIML in the estimation process, or does it use listwise deletion?

It doesn't do either. Your model was already fitted using lavaan() or one of the wrapper functions like growth().  lavInspect() simply calculates the correlations implied by the estimated model parameters.  Whether FIML or listwise deletion was used to estimate those parameters, you can see in your own syntax, or afterward by calling lavInspect(fit, "options")$missing
